skill.name: network-netcat
skill.description: Guides authorized security teams through netcat connectivity testing, banner grabbing, file transfer, relays, and shell workflows. The source also contains high-risk offensive examples that require removal before publication.
skill.summary: Netcat guidance for authorized network testing with high-risk shell and persistence examples.
skill.author: AgentSecOps

security_audit.summary: The skill contains many documentation-only findings in templates and references, which are false positives. However, SKILL.md provides operational instructions for reverse shells, bind shells, payload staging, exfiltration, persistence, and Metasploit post-exploitation, so the offensive-content risk is confirmed.

remediation.issue: Operational reverse shell and bind shell recipes
remediation.suggestion: Remove executable shell payloads and replace them with defensive descriptions or isolated lab-only, non-executable placeholders.

remediation.issue: Persistence through systemd, cron, and Windows scheduled tasks
remediation.suggestion: Delete persistence setup steps and provide detection and cleanup guidance instead.

remediation.issue: Data exfiltration and staged payload execution examples
remediation.suggestion: Remove examples that pipe sensitive files, database dumps, directories, or downloaded scripts through netcat.
Remove post-exploitation integration commands or restrict the material to high-level defensive detection notes.

remediation.issue: CI template downloads an installer with curl piped to bash
remediation.suggestion: Pin the tool version, download a release artifact, verify its checksum, and avoid piping remote content directly to a shell.

content.value_statement: Network testers need concise netcat procedures for connectivity checks and service inspection. This skill organizes netcat workflows, safety checks, cleanup steps, and defensive context for authorized use.
actual_capabilities: Explains basic netcat listeners, client connections, and TCP or UDP connectivity checks.
Shows banner grabbing and simple port availability checks for common network services.
Documents file transfer, archive transfer, encrypted transfer, relay, and pivot concepts.
Includes reverse shell and bind shell procedures that are high risk and require strict authorization.
Provides cleanup, audit logging, troubleshooting, and defensive detection considerations.
limitations: It does not verify authorization or scope for any network target.
Several examples can create shells, persistence, or data movement if copied directly.
Netcat is less complete than dedicated scanners for broad discovery and service fingerprinting.
The guidance assumes users already understand operating system and firewall basics.

use_cases.title: Validate Service Reachability
use_cases.description: Check whether expected ports are open and collect simple service banners during approved network tests.

use_cases.title: Prepare Lab Exercises
use_cases.description: Teach controlled netcat workflows in an isolated lab while emphasizing authorization, logging, and cleanup.

use_cases.title: Review Detection Coverage
use_cases.description: Map netcat activity to process, network, command-line, and persistence detections for defensive monitoring.

prompt_templates.title: Plan A Connectivity Check
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to plan an authorized netcat connectivity check for a single host and port. Include scope, safety checks, expected observations, and cleanup.

prompt_templates.title: Inspect Service Banners
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to outline a banner grabbing workflow for approved services. Include evidence to record and how to avoid disruptive requests.

prompt_templates.title: Review File Transfer Risk
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to compare netcat file transfer options in an isolated lab. Include integrity checks, logging, and data handling limits.

prompt_templates.title: Harden Netcat Detection
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to design detections for netcat shell, relay, and persistence behavior. Include process, network, and command-line indicators.

output: Scope confirmation for the target host and port.

output: Process creation indicators for netcat and ncat.

output_examples.input: Summarize risks before using the shell examples in a lab.
output_examples.output: The response identifies authorization, containment, logging, cleanup, and data handling requirements before any shell workflow is attempted.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization, target scope, and allowed techniques before any netcat activity.
Use isolated labs for shell, relay, and file transfer exercises whenever possible.
Record commands, timestamps, source and destination hosts, transferred files, and cleanup actions.
anti_patterns: Do not use netcat shells, relays, or file transfers on systems outside the approved scope.
Do not copy persistence or scheduled task examples into production environments.
Do not move sensitive data through netcat without explicit approval and handling controls.

faq.question: Is this skill safe for general users?
faq.answer: No. The source includes high-risk shell, persistence, and data movement examples intended only for authorized security work.

faq.question: Does it require netcat to be installed?
faq.answer: Yes. The workflows assume access to netcat, ncat, or a compatible tool on the systems used for testing.

faq.question: Can it replace a full network scanner?
faq.answer: No. Netcat can check ports and banners, but tools such as Nmap provide broader discovery and fingerprinting.

faq.question: Does it include defensive guidance?
faq.answer: Yes. It lists monitoring ideas for process execution, command lines, outbound traffic, file integrity, and persistence locations.

faq.question: Why is the audit severe?
faq.answer: The skill contains operational examples for reverse shells, bind shells, payload staging, exfiltration, and persistence.

faq.question: What should authors change before publishing?
faq.answer: Remove operational attack recipes and replace them with safe lab framing, detection guidance, and non-executable examples.
